title: Message Submission for Mail
subtitle: Why your mail program hands outgoing mail to a submission server on port 587 instead of dropping it into the open mail network.
summary: RFC 6409 defines message submission: the step where a mail program (a Message User Agent) hands a new message to a Message Submission Agent, normally over port 587. It uses ordinary ESMTP but adds rules for the server: it must require authentication, make sure every domain is fully qualified, and may fix up or reject the message. Keeping submission apart from relay lets a site apply stricter policy at the point where mail enters the network. It is a full Internet Standard (STD 72) and replaces RFC 4409.

eli5.summary: Think of a post office with two doors. One door is for mail that is already on its way between post offices. The other door is for you, where a clerk checks who you are, checks the address is complete, and only then puts your letter in the system.

questions: what is a message submission agent
what is the difference between port 25 and port 587
why does my email server require authentication to send
what is the difference between submission and relay

tldr.problem: SMTP was built to move finished messages between servers, yet it was also being used by mail programs to inject new messages, with no good place to check who is sending or to fix incomplete messages.
tldr.mechanism: Mail programs connect to a Message Submission Agent on port 587 using ESMTP. The MSA must require SMTP authentication by default and keep envelope domains fully qualified, and it may reject, complete or rewrite the message before passing it on.
tldr.outcome: Submission and relay get separate policies, so sites can control who sends mail and block outbound spam from infected machines. Port 587 with authentication is how most mail clients send mail today.

today: Port 587 is the standard way mail clients send mail to their provider, and most hosted mail services accept authenticated submission there. RFC 8314, which updates this RFC, goes further and recommends submission over TLS from the first byte, using implicit TLS on port 465, instead of the plain connection plus STARTTLS that RFC 6409 describes. Many networks also block outbound port 25 from ordinary users so that mail must go through a submission server, the practice this RFC's introduction describes.

implementations.name: Postfix (submission service)
implementations.note: Commonly configured to listen on port 587 as a separate submission service with authentication required.

implementations.name: Exim
implementations.note: Widely deployed mail server that can run an authenticated submission listener on port 587.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SMTP, defined in RFC 5321, was designed as a message transfer protocol: a way to route and deliver finished messages from one mail server to the next. Over time it also became the way people's mail programs introduce brand-new messages into the mail system. That is submission, and the server that accepts it is called a Message Submission Agent (MSA).

To permit unconstrained communication, SMTP is often not authenticated during relay, so that anyone's mail can reach anyone. That openness is a poor fit for the first hop. Submitted messages are also often unfinished: a missing Date header, a domain that is not fully qualified, or a client that does not know its own time zone. The RFC says that completing messages later, in downstream transfer agents, has been shown to cause harm.

RFC 6409 therefore describes a low-cost, deterministic way to identify submissions and states what a submission server must do. It is the revision of RFC 4409, which in turn updated RFC 2476.

Transfer
Server to server, mostly unauthenticated, finished messages (SMTP, RFC 5321).
Submission
Mail program to its own server, authenticated, messages may need finishing (this RFC).
sections.eli5: Your letter first goes to your own mailbox clerk, who checks it is really from you and that the address is complete. After that it travels between post offices without further questions.

sections.title: Identifying a Submission
sections.content:
The RFC makes identification simple: port 587 is reserved for message submission, and any message received on that port is by definition a submission. The protocol on that port is ESMTP, the extended SMTP from RFC 5321, with the extra restrictions and allowances this RFC lists.

Using a separate port is the "low-cost, deterministic" means mentioned in the introduction. A server does not have to guess whether a connection comes from a mail program or from another server, because the port number says so. Sites that cannot move clients to port 587 may still use port 25 for submission, as long as some hosts are designated as MSAs and others as MTAs.

The RFC also lets MTAs and MSAs apply different rejection rules. For example, a site might make its MTA reject any RCPT command for a non-local recipient, while its MSA rejects any submission that does not come from an authorized user. A null return path, MAIL FROM:<>, is allowed on submission and must not by itself be a reason to reject, since mail programs need it for things such as disposition notifications.
sections.eli5: The submission door has a number on it, 587. Anything that comes through that door is known to be a new letter being handed in, not one passing through.

sections.title: Authorized Submission
sections.content:
Section 3.3 reviews how a site can make sure only authorized users submit mail: authenticated SMTP, IP address restrictions, secure IP and other tunnels, and prior POP authentication.

The RFC singles out SMTP AUTH (RFC 4954) as widely deployed, because it gives the MSA an authorization identity that is not tied to other protocols. IP address restrictions are common but do not help travelers and can be spoofed unless every network path between client and server is trustworthy. Secure IP and similar tunnels add protection against eavesdropping and traffic analysis. Requiring a recent POP login from the same IP address works, but it forces clients to log in to POP before sending, makes the MSA coordinate with the POP server, and leaves a window during which someone else on that address can submit mail.

The mechanisms are not equally strong. Prior POP authentication depends on the client's IP address, so it is "substantially as subject to IP address spoofing" as validation based on known IP addresses alone, in the RFC's words.
sections.eli5: There are several ways the clerk can know you are allowed in: you show a password, you are standing inside the building, or you came through a private tunnel. Showing a password works best when you are away from home.

sections.title: What a Submission Server Must, Should and May Do
sections.content:
The core of the RFC is three lists. An MSA MUST use reply code 554 to reject a MAIL, RCPT or DATA command that contains something improper, ensure that all domains in the SMTP envelope are fully qualified, and, by default, give an error response to MAIL if the session has not been authenticated with SMTP AUTH. Reply code 530 is used for that last case, unless authentication or authorization was already established some other way, such as by being inside a protected subnetwork.

It SHOULD reject illegal address syntax (reply code 501 for a detectably improper address in MAIL or RCPT), log message errors, especially apparent client misconfigurations, and answer every command, even DATA, in under 2 minutes. It MAY enforce submission rights and recipient permissions (reply code 550 with an enhanced status code such as 5.7.1), check message data, relax authentication for the postmaster address, and convert character encodings.

If the MSA cannot determine a return path for the submitter, it SHOULD reject immediately with 550 on the MAIL command. For other rejections it may either reject right away or accept the message and send a bounce later; the RFC prefers immediate rejection because it gives the user direct feedback.
sections.eli5: The clerk must check your ID and make sure the address is complete. The clerk should also be quick and keep notes about mistakes. The clerk is allowed to do extra things, like tidying up your handwriting.

sections.title: Interaction with SMTP Extensions
sections.content:
Many SMTP extensions say nothing about whether they apply to submission. Section 7 settles this with Table 1, which lists extensions whose own documents are silent and says whether each applies on the submission port. The table also corrects and extends the IANA registry of SMTP service extensions (section 10).

Three points stand out. AUTH is a MUST: an MSA has to support SMTP authentication. PIPELINING, ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES and 8BITMIME are SHOULD. ETRN and ATRN, which let a client ask a server to start sending queued mail, are MUST NOT on the submission port, as is the 521 reply code. STARTTLS is a MAY, and the RFC calls it the most widely used way to protect submission integrity and privacy at the time of writing.

Future extensions SHOULD say explicitly whether they are valid on the submission port. Any reference to the DATA command also covers substitutes such as BDAT with CHUNKING.
sections.eli5: SMTP has lots of add-on features. This part is a checklist saying which ones the submission door must offer, which are nice to have and which are not allowed.

sections.title: Message Modifications
sections.content:
Because submission is the first hop, a site may repair or adjust messages here. The RFC lists, and calls "often considered useful", the following changes. The MSA MAY add or replace a Sender field if the sender's identity is known and is not in From, add or correct a Date field, apply MIME transfer encoding, sign the message, encrypt it, resolve aliases such as CNAME records, and rewrite local parts or domains by local policy. It SHOULD add or replace a missing or invalid Message-ID.

The RFC adds guardrails. Limit changes to specific problems with clear solutions; blindly appending a domain to every unqualified address "typically results in more broken addresses". Rewrite only addresses that match specific local configuration, never with data-independent rules. Anything the MSA forwards MUST still conform to RFC 5321 and RFC 5322.

Modifying a message can invalidate an existing DKIM, PGP or S/MIME signature, which may change how later receivers treat it. This warning was added in RFC 6409.
sections.eli5: If your letter is missing a date or a return address, the clerk can add it. The clerk should only fix clear mistakes, because changing a sealed letter can break its seal.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security case for this RFC is that separating submission from relay lets a site apply different policies to each, and that doing so is simpler technically and administratively, which makes it more likely the policies are applied correctly. It can also help track and prevent unsolicited bulk email.

The RFC's example is a site where the MSA requires authentication before accepting a message while the MTA rejects every RCPT command for a non-local user. If a site requires no authorization at all for submissions, it allows open use of its resources and name, and spam can be injected through its facilities.

Two cautions are repeated from earlier sections. Some authentication methods are weaker than others (section 3). And logging of client errors has to be limited, because unlimited logging can enable certain denial-of-service attacks (section 5.2 of the RFC, covered above under what the server should do). A related caution in the extensions discussion is that a rejection can reveal local security policy, so no more detail than needed should be given to unauthenticated senders.
sections.eli5: Two doors mean two sets of rules. The submission door checks everyone's ID, so strangers cannot use your post office to send junk.

items.title: SMTP AUTH
items.text: Widely deployed; gives the MSA an authorization identity that is not tied to other protocols.

items.title: IP address restrictions
items.text: Very common, but no help for travelers and easy to spoof unless the whole path is trusted.

items.title: Secure IP and tunnels
items.text: Add protection against eavesdropping and traffic analysis.

items.title: Prior POP authentication
items.text: Needs a recent POP login from the same IP; the client and server must coordinate, and a spoofing window remains.

data.title: Illustrative submission session (example.net)
data.code:
C: (connect to submit.example.net, port 587)
S: 220 submit.example.net ESMTP ready
C: EHLO client.example.net
S: 250-submit.example.net
S: 250-AUTH PLAIN
S: 250 ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES
C: MAIL FROM:<alice@example.net>
S: 530 5.7.0 Authentication required
   ... client authenticates with AUTH, then retries ...
C: MAIL FROM:<alice@example.net>
S: 250 2.1.0 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<bob@example.org>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: DATA
S: 354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>
C: (message text; the MSA may add Date or Message-ID)
S: 250 2.0.0 Ok: queued
